Balancing Memory Pathways: Analyzing and Improving Memory Utilization in Hybrid LMs

Hyunji Lee ††thanks: Correspondence to: hyunjil@cs.unc.edu Affiliation: UNC Chapel Hill    Joykirat Singh Affiliation: UNC Chapel Hill    Zaid Khan Affiliation: UNC Chapel Hill    Justin Chih-Yao Chen Affiliation: UNC Chapel Hill    Elias Stengel-Eskin Affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin    Alessandro Sordoni Affiliation: Mila    Arman Cohan Affiliation: Yale University    Mohit Bansal Affiliation: UNC Chapel Hill
Abstract

Recurrent–attention hybrid language models (LMs), which interleave attention and recurrent layers, are increasingly used to combine the efficiency of the recurrent layers with the strong performance of attention layers. Prior work suggests that attention and recurrent layers offer complementary pathways to use past information: attention supports precise memory recall from earlier tokens, while recurrent layers support consolidation of disparate information over long contexts. However, we observe that simply having access to both pathways does not mean that hybrid LMs are effectively using them. When we analyze how much the models rely on each pathway, we find a substantially greater reliance on attention than on the recurrent state. Standard supervised fine-tuning improves overall performance but does not improve how the two memory pathways are coordinated: the model becomes more reliant on information propagated by attention layers, while its use of information propagated by recurrent layers remains limited. To encourage better coordination between the two memory pathways, we add an auxiliary loss that limits attention’s access to earlier context while the recurrent state propagates through the full sequence. This objective encourages the model to retain and use information through the recurrent pathway alongside attention. It improves overall performance, with particularly strong gains on tasks involving longer contexts or requiring information aggregation, consistent with the strengths of recurrent layers observed in analysis. Crucially, this imbalance and the benefit of our auxiliary loss generalize: they apply to multiple recurrent-attention LMs in question-answering and agentic tasks, as well as to attention-based LMs that combine different forms of memory. Together, our findings show that simply providing multiple memory pathways does not ensure their effective use, and that targeted supervision is needed to better coordinate them.11 1 Code in https://github.com/amy-hyunji/Balancing-Memory-Pathways

1 Introduction

Recurrent–attention hybrid language models (Qwen Team, 2026; Ren et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2024; NVIDIA et al., 2025), which consist of recurrent and attention layers, leverage efficient recurrent computation and expressive attention memory to allow flexible access to prior context. These architectures contain two memory pathways for retaining and using past information: attention and recurrent layers. Prior work (Lee et al., 2025; Michalak and Abreu, 2025; Bick et al., 2026) has analyzed distinct characteristics and strengths of these components: attention layers support precise memory recall by directly accessing earlier information, while recurrent layers synthesize information distributed across long contexts. Extending these findings, we observe that attention plays a larger role when the answer appears directly in the context or can be found from a single piece of evidence, whereas the recurrent state plays a larger role when the answer must be inferred rather than copied or requires combining multiple pieces of evidence across the context. These complementary strengths motivate an important question: How well do hybrid LMs use both memory pathways, and how can their coordination be improved?

We first examine how existing hybrid LMs use their attention and recurrent memory pathways. We find that having both pathways does not mean that models use both effectively; models retain most of their accuracy even when the recurrent pathway’s access to past information is limited (30.2% →\rightarrow 20.2%), whereas accuracy drops substantially when the same restriction is applied to attention layers (30.2% →\rightarrow 5.1%). This imbalance in memory utilization persists even after standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on downstream tasks such as question answering. Although the overall performance improves, the gains are mostly from better utilization of attention layers whereas their use of the recurrent pathway remains limited (Figure 1, Standard SFT box).

To address this imbalance in memory utilization, we add an auxiliary loss that complements standard SFT by encouraging the model to retain and use information through the recurrent pathway. In an auxiliary forward pass, we restrict the attention layers’ access to past context, requiring the model to access it through recurrent states. This simple intervention improves question-answering performance, with average absolute accuracy gains of 3.9% on Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026) and 5.2% on Nemotron-H-4B-Instruct (NVIDIA et al., 2025) across six datasets. Adding the auxiliary loss also substantially improves performance when past information is propagated only through recurrent layers, suggesting increased use of recurrent memory. The gains are particularly large on longer-context datasets (8.0%) compared to shorter context (0.2%), consistent with more effective use of recurrent layers’ previously identified strength in processing long contexts. Reversing the restriction to encourage attention leads to smaller gains, suggesting that the improvement from the auxiliary loss depends on which pathway is encouraged, with greater improvement from strengthening the underutilized recurrent pathway (Figure 1, With Auxiliary Loss box).

The benefits of auxiliary supervision also extend to agentic tasks, where agents must explore, accumulate observations, and use them to choose subsequent actions. When averaged across both models, adding recurrent auxiliary supervision improves the success rate by 3.5% and 9.3% on Quest and Treasure tasks in TextWorld (Côté et al., 2019), and by 22.0% and 13.5% on the PutNextLocal and GoToObjMaze tasks in BabyAI (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2019), respectively. We observe that the larger gains on BabyAI mirror our question answering results, where the auxiliary loss tends to show stronger improvement on longer contexts; BabyAI trajectories (avg. 134.0 steps) are substantially longer compared to TextWorld (avg. 42.2 steps).

We further examine how the auxiliary loss affects the use of past information. When models are allowed to retry after failures, with their previous attempts stored in memory so that they can revise their answers or actions (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024), models trained with the auxiliary loss recover more successfully, improving the cumulative recovery rate over standard SFT by 16.6% on question answering and 19.2% on agentic tasks. In question answering, the gain is especially large on multi-evidence questions compared to single-evidence questions (30.3% vs. 2.8%). We attribute this to the auxiliary loss encouraging greater use of recurrent layers, which we observe to play a larger role in multi-evidence questions. In the agentic setup, when given multiple suboptimal successful demonstrations, we observe that agents trained with the auxiliary loss more often generate trajectories shorter than any provided demonstrations (6.0% on average), with larger gains when the demonstrations are longer. Finally, the same imbalance and the strength of the auxiliary loss generalize to attention-based LMs with multiple memories: standard SFT favors one memory pathway over another, and adding auxiliary supervision that encourages the use of the underutilized pathway increases usage of the pathway and improves overall performance in question-answering. Across architectures and tasks, our findings highlight that simply providing multiple memory pathways does not lead to balanced, complementary use; models must instead be trained to coordinate these memory pathways.

2 Background & Related Work

In this section, we provide an overview of recurrent-attention hybrid LMs in Section 2.1, then review and extend prior findings on the roles of the recurrent and attention memory pathways in Section 2.2.

2.1 Recurrent-Attention Hybrid LMs

Recurrent-attention hybrid LMs (Ren et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2024; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026) integrate attention and recurrent layers to combine strong language modeling performance with computational efficiency. An attention layer computes each token’s representation by attending to the current and preceding tokens, providing direct access to past information at the cost of quadratic computation in sequence length and KV cache that grows linearly. A linear recurrent layer, such as Mamba2 (Dao and Gu, 2024) or Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025), instead updates a fixed-size state as new tokens are processed, enabling computation that scales linearly with sequence length and constant memory size. Throughout the paper, we refer to such linear recurrent layers simply as recurrent layers. Many hybrid LMs interleave these layers, combining attention’s direct access to earlier tokens with recurrent layers’ compact integration of past information (Kimi Team et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025). These models often match or outperform fully attention-based models despite using relatively few attention layers, while gaining efficiency from the larger portion of recurrent layers.

2.2 Roles and Strengths of Attention and Recurrent Memory Pathways

Findings from Prior Work.

Prior work has identified distinct roles for attention and recurrent components in hybrid LMs. Attention is particularly important for precise retrieval, where removing attention causes severe retrieval failure in the evaluated hybrids (Michalak and Abreu, 2025; Bick et al., 2026). Recurrent components contribute substantially to language modeling, where removing the recurrent pathway causes larger degradations in likelihood-based evaluation than removing attention (Lee et al., 2025; Borobia et al., 2026). While these studies characterize the distinct strengths of the two memory pathways, they do not analyze whether hybrid LMs make effective use of both pathways’ strengths or how to improve their use.

Revisiting and Extending Prior Findings.

We first revisit the distinct roles of attention and recurrent layers identified in the studies reviewed above. Following the setup from Lee et al. (2025), we use Based NQ (Arora et al., 2024) to evaluate memory recall and PG19 (Rae et al., 2019) to evaluate language modeling, and measure the increase in negative log-likelihood (NLL) when either attention or recurrent layers are ablated relative to the unablated model using Qwen3.5. Figure 3 shows a pattern consistent with prior findings: on retrieval QA, ablating attention increases NLL more than ablating recurrent layers (5.3 vs. 1.5). The pattern reverses for language modeling, where ablating recurrent layers has a larger effect (1.3 vs. 3.7). This contrast suggests that attention contributes more to precise recall, while recurrent layers contribute more to aggregating information across the context.

We then extend the analysis to different question types to test whether the two memory pathways have distinct roles or strengths for different information needs using the datasets described in Section 3. We consider two distinctions. First, we classify a question as verbatim if its normalized gold answer appears in the source context, and as non-verbatim otherwise. Second, we classify questions as single-evidence or multi-evidence based on the number of evidence required to answer them, where evidence annotations are available. We match the number of examples across the two categories in each distinction. Figure 3 compares pathway use across question types. We measure attention-only retention as the fraction of full-model accuracy preserved when cross-context information is accessible only through attention layers; higher retention indicates greater reliance on attention and less on recurrent state. We observe that retention is higher for verbatim than non-verbatim questions (63% vs. 46%) and for single-evidence than multi-evidence questions (60% vs. 50%). This aligns with the findings above: attention layers play a larger role in recovering precise details, but contribute less when information must be abstracted or integrated across the context. Further details are in Appendix A.

3 Experimental Setup

Models.

We experiment over two recurrent-attention hybrid LMs: Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026) and Nemotron-H-4B-Instruct (NVIDIA et al., 2025). Qwen3.5-4B contains 24 Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025) and 8 full-attention layers. Nemotron-H-4B-Instruct consists of 24 Mamba2 (Dao and Gu, 2024) and 4 full-attention layers.

Training.

We train all models using LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) on all layers with rank 16, scaling factor 32, and dropout 0.05. We use AdamW with a learning rate of 1​e−41e^{-4}, a cosine learning rate schedule, a warmup period covering 3% of training steps, and an effective batch size of 16. Since objectives with an auxiliary loss require additional computation, we halve the number of optimization steps to match the total training compute with standard SFT. Unless otherwise specified, we use the same optimization setting across all compared variants.

Task & Evaluations.

We experiment on long-context question answering and long-horizon agentic tasks, which are two common settings for studying memory in which the model needs to retain and use information from earlier contexts or interactions for strong performance (Packer et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024; Shinn et al., 2023). For Question Answering, we pool training examples from four datasets so that the model is trained over diverse context lengths and reasoning types: DROP (Dua et al., 2019), HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), Qasper (Dasigi et al., 2021), NarrativeQA (Kočiský et al., 2017). This yields 12k training and 2k validation instances. We evaluate each dataset separately, and additionally evaluate on MINTEval (Lee et al., 2026) and MuSR (Sprague et al., 2024), leading to a total of 8.2k test examples with an average context length of 84k tokens. For Agentic Tasks, we experiment over TextWorld (Côté et al., 2019) and BabyAI (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2019), where agents must explore the environment, accumulate information through sequences of observations and actions, and use it to make subsequent decisions. The environments differ in their observation spaces, action spaces, and in the structure of their trajectories. In TextWorld, we train on Quest and evaluate on both Quest and Treasure. In BabyAI, we train on MiniBossLevel and evaluate on PutNextLocal and GoToObjMaze. Further details are in Appendix B.

4 Standard SFT Favors Attention over Recurrence

In Section 2.2, we observed complementary strengths and roles of the two pathways: attention supports precise recall, while recurrent layers integrate information across the context. Thus, in this section, we examine whether standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) leads the model to use both pathways in ways that leverage these complementary strengths. We first define attention-only and recurrent-only conditions to analyze and assess the model’s use of each memory pathway (Section 4.1). We then evaluate how overall performance and pathway utilization change after SFT on question answering and agentic tasks (Section 4.2).

4.1 Disentangling two memory pathways

To analyze how past information is carried through attention and recurrence, we divide each input into a past portion and a current portion, and selectively restrict which memory mechanism can transfer information from the past to the current input. For example, in question answering, the past portion corresponds to the context and the current portion to the question. We use full to denote the unmodified condition, in which both attention and recurrent layers can propagate information from the past to the current portion. We construct two complementary interventions, recurrent-only and attention-only; these indicate which mechanism can carry information from the past to the current portion. In the recurrent-only setting, attention cannot access the past portion, so past information reaches the current portion only through the recurrent state; the attention-only setting does the opposite. In both, all layers remain active within each portion.

Specifically, in the recurrent-only condition, we block attention across segment boundaries while allowing the recurrent state to propagate normally:

Mt,s={0,s≤t​ and ​σ​(s)=σ⁡(t),−∞,otherwise.M_{t,s}=\begin{cases}0,&s\leq t\text{ and }\sigma(s)=\sigma(t),\\ -\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Mt,sM_{t,s} is added to the attention score between query position tt and key position ss before normalization, and σ⁡(t)\sigma(t) denotes the segment containing token tt. The mask therefore retains standard causal attention within each segment, while blocking attention to all tokens in preceding segments.

Conversely, in the attention-only condition, we retain the standard causal attention over the preceding context, while restricting the recurrent state from propagating across segment boundaries (σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot)). For t>1t>1, we modify the recurrent update as:

St=[σ(t)=σ(t−1)]𝒜t(St−1)+wt,S0=0,S_{t}=\mathbb{1}\!\left[\sigma(t)=\sigma(t-1)\right]\mathcal{A}_{t}(S_{t-1})+w_{t},\qquad S_{0}=0,

where StS_{t} denotes the recurrent state after processing token tt, 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} denotes the recurrent transition applied to the previous state, wtw_{t} denotes the contribution of the current token, and 𝟙​[⋅]\mathbb{1}[\cdot] denotes an indicator function. At a segment boundary (σ⁡(t)≠σ⁡(t−1)\sigma(t)\neq\sigma(t-1)), the indicator is zero, so the previous recurrent state does not contribute to the new segment and within a segment, the recurrent update is unchanged. Thus, information from preceding segments remains accessible only through attention.

4.2 Memory Pathway Utilization after SFT

We evaluate both the original and SFT-trained models under the full, attention-only, and recurrent-only conditions defined in Section 4.1. As shown in Figure 5, the SFT-trained model (Standard SFT) achieves 34.6% QA accuracy on Qwen3.5 under the full condition, compared to 30.2% for the original model (Base). Attention-only accuracy also increases from 20.2% to 25.0%, whereas recurrent-only accuracy remains nearly unchanged (5.1% to 5.0%). We observe a similar pattern on the agentic Quest task: full success rate rises from 27.0% to 78.5%, attention-only also rises from 6.0% to 52.0%, while recurrent-only improves only slightly, from 2.5% to 4.0%. These results indicate that the model retains a large portion of its full performance when recurrent layers are restricted to local information (attention-only), but drops sharply when attention is restricted to local information (recurrent-only). This gap widens after SFT.

This shift toward the attention pathway also appears across the question types discussed in Section 2.2. We observe that attention-only retention, the fraction of full-model accuracy preserved under the attention-only condition, increases for all question types (Figure 5). The gain is larger for question types that already relied more on attention: verbatim and single-evidence questions show an average increase of 25.5% compared to 19.2% for non-verbatim and multi-evidence questions.

Together, these results show that standard SFT improves overall performance but does not lead to balanced use of the two memory pathways: the model becomes more reliant on attention, while its use of recurrent pathway changes little. Given the distinct strengths of these pathways observed in Section 2.2, we next investigate whether encouraging more effective use of both pathways can improve memory coordination and further enhance overall performance.

5 Encouraging Recurrent Memory Use Improves Performance

In Section 2.2, we observe that attention and recurrent layers play complementary roles, each carrying important information for different types of questions. However, Section 4.2 shows that standard SFT does not effectively utilize both pathways, instead increasing the model’s reliance on attention while leaving the recurrent pathway underutilized. Thus, in this section, we examine whether adding auxiliary loss that encourages the use of recurrent pathway (Section 5.1) leads to better memory coordination and stronger overall performance (Section 5.2).

5.1 Recurrent Auxiliary Supervision

We augment standard SFT with an auxiliary loss that uses the same supervised next-token prediction objective but masks attention to the preceding context, a mechanism commonly used to control information flow in LMs (Mu et al., 2024; Dong et al., 2019). Unlike attention, recurrent layers remain unrestricted: they process the entire sequence and propagate their state from the preceding context. Thus, during the auxiliary forward pass, information from the preceding context can influence the answer only through recurrent memory, encouraging the model to retain and use information throughout the recurrent pathway. We jointly optimize the standard SFT loss (ℒSFT​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)), computed without these restrictions, and the auxiliary loss (ℒrec​(θ)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}(\theta)):

ℒ⁡(θ)=ℒSFT​(θ)+λ​ℒrec​(θ),\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}(\theta),

where θ\theta denotes model parameters and λ\lambda controls the strength of the auxiliary supervision.22 2 Ablation of different λ\lambda in Appendix C.1

5.2 Results

Question Answering.

Table 1 shows accuracy across six question-answering datasets. When comparing standard SFT (LS​F​TL_{SFT}) with when adding auxiliary recurrent supervision (LS​F​TL_{SFT}+Lr​e​cL_{rec}), we observe that adding recurrent auxiliary loss improves the average accuracy from 34.6% to 38.5% in Qwen3.5 and from 31.0% to 36.2% in Nemotron-H. The gains are particularly large on Qasper, NarrativeQA, and MINTEval, suggesting that the auxiliary loss is especially helpful for answering questions from longer contexts. Figure 6 further shows that adding recurrent auxiliary supervision substantially improves recurrent-only accuracy (5.0% to 22.8%) while largely preserving attention-only accuracy (25.0% to 23.7%), suggesting more effective use of recurrent state. This improved utilization, together with the recurrent pathway’s strength in aggregating information across long contexts observed in Section 2.2, suggests that more effective use of recurrent state contributes to the overall performance gains.

To understand which part of the objective drives these gains, we conduct analysis with several training variants. For these ablations, we consider La​t​t​nL_{attn}, which is the counterpart of Lr​e​cL_{rec}: it blocks recurrent-state propagation from the preceding context while leaving attention unrestricted. We compare training with auxiliary losses alone (Lr​e​cL_{rec} or La​t​t​nL_{attn}), and adding La​t​t​nL_{attn} to standard SFT (LS​F​T+La​t​t​nL_{SFT}+L_{attn}). We observe that LS​F​T+La​t​t​nL_{SFT}+L_{attn} yields a smaller gain than LS​F​T+Lr​e​cL_{SFT}+L_{rec} for both models, with average absolute improvement of 2.1% and 4.6%, respectively. Figure 6 further shows that adding La​t​t​nL_{attn} increases attention-only accuracy from 25.0% to 28.0%, while recurrent-only accuracy remains much lower at 11.3%, indicating continued imbalance between the two memory pathways. These results suggest that strengthening the underutilized recurrent pathway is more effective than further encouraging the use of attention. Finally, training with only the auxiliary loss (La​t​t​nL_{attn} or Lr​e​cL_{rec}) yields lower average accuracy than standard SFT (LS​F​TL_{SFT}) when averaged over both models, by 1.3% and 2.7%, respectively. This suggests that restricted losses are most effective as auxiliary objectives alongside unrestricted SFT.

Agentic Tasks.

Table 2 shows performance on two agentic tasks: TextWorld and BabyAI. We observe similar trend as we observed from question answering task: when adding recurrent auxiliary supervision to standard SFT (ℒSFT+ℒrec\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}), it improves success rate over standard SFT (ℒSFT\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}) by a large gain: when averaged across Qwen3.5 and Nemotron-H, the absolute gains are 3.5% and 9.3% in TextWorld Quest and Treasure, respectively, and 22.0% and 13.5% in BabyAI PutNextLocal and GoToObjMaze, respectively. Similarly, ℒSFT+ℒattn\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{attn}} yields a smaller gain than ℒSFT+ℒrec\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} across all four games, with average absolute improvements of 4.1% and 12.1%, respectively. The larger gains on BabyAI are consistent with our question-answering results, where recurrent auxiliary supervision is particularly beneficial on longer-context datasets. BabyAI trajectories are generally longer than those in TextWorld, averaging 134.0 versus 42.2 steps across all trajectories and 40.2 versus 13.8 steps among successful trajectories.

6 Auxiliary Supervision Generalizes

In this section, we examine whether encouraging the use of the recurrent pathway also improves the model’s ability to learn from past failure and successful trajectories (Zhao et al., 2024; Shinn et al., 2023). We then examine whether our observations generalize to attention-based LMs with multiple memories.

Learning from Failure Trajectories.

We analyze whether models can recover from their own errors when given additional attempts, with previous failed attempts provided in context (Shinn et al., 2023; Gou et al., 2024). For question answering, we evaluate on MINTEval, which includes long contexts and both single-evidence and multi-evidence questions about the same context. Figure 7 (left) shows the cumulative recovery rate (y-axis) as the maximum number of attempts (x-axis) increases. Across all questions (solid lines), recovery rates increase with additional attempts under both standard SFT and SFT with auxiliary loss. Adding the auxiliary loss consistently improves recovery, with an average absolute gain of 16.6% across attempt budgets. The gains are particularly large on multi-evidence questions: averaged across attempt budgets, recovery improves from 27.3% to 57.6%, compared to 14.8% to 17.6% on single-evidence questions. For agentic tasks, we apply the same retry setup to TextWorld, providing previous failed trajectories in context. The auxiliary loss improves cumulative recovery by an average of 19.2% (Figure 10 in Appendix). Recovery continues to improve with additional attempts under SFT with the auxiliary loss, whereas standard SFT plateaus. These results suggest that the auxiliary loss helps models more effectively use failed attempts stored in memory to recover from errors.

Learning from Successful Trajectories.

We examine whether agents can use successful but suboptimal trajectoreis to develop more efficient strategies. We provide multiple successful demonstrations of varying lenghts, which may contain unnecessary steps, and measure how often the agent generates a successful trajectory shorter than the shortest demonstration. As shown in Figure 7 (right), adding the auxiliary loss improves this rate by an average of 6.0%, with larger gains as demonstrations length increases relative to the optimal path. These results suggest that the auxiliary loss helps agents more effectively use successful demonstrations stored in memory to develop more efficient strategies.

Generalizes to Attention-Based LMs.

We find that both the imbalance in memory use and the benefits of auxiliary supervision extend to attention-based LMs with multiple memory types (textual and latent memory). As shown in Figure 8, standard SFT (SFT) with both memories achieves 24.1% accuracy, far below the Oracle, which selects the better of the two single-memory predictions for each example (32.0%) and even below the text-only model (25.9%). This suggests that access to both memories does not ensure effective use of their complementary strengths. Even when trained jointly with standard SFT, the model remains biased toward using textual memory. Adding an auxiliary loss that encourages the use of both memory pathways improves accuracy to 28.6%. Further analysis shows that this improvement is accompanied by increased use of latent memory while largely preserving use of textual memory (Appendix C.3).

7 Conclusion

In this paper, we show that recurrent-attention hybrid LMs tend to rely predominantly on the attention pathway despite the complementary strengths of their recurrent layers, and that standard SFT further increases attention use while yielding little improvement in recurrent memory use. We show that adding a simple auxiliary loss that encourages use of the recurrent pathway improves utilization of both memory pathways and overall performance. These findings generalize across multiple recurrent-attention hybrid LMs, across question answering and agentic tasks, and to attention-based LMs that combine different forms of memory.

Appendix A Details on Role analysis of hybrid LMs

A.1 Verbatim vs. Non-Verbatim Questions

We first distinguish questions based on whether their answers can be directly recovered from the source context. We define a question as verbatim when its normalized gold answer appears in the source document and non-verbatim otherwise. Approximately 34.6% of the test examples (about 2.8k examples) are verbatim and to match the number of instances for the two categories, we randomly sample the same number of examples from the remaining non-verbatim questions.

A.2 Single- vs. Multi-Evidence Questions

We next examine whether the relative strengths of the two memory pathways change with the amount of evidence required to answer a question. Using the evidence annotations provided by the datasets, we divide questions into those that rely on a single piece of evidence and those that require multiple pieces of evidence. Among the test examples, approximately 30.2% (about 2.5k) are single-evidence and 39.7% (about 3.3k) are multi-evidence, and the rest does not provide explicit evidence annotations. To balance the two categories, we randomly sample the same number of multi-evidence questions as single-evidence ones, resulting in around 2.5k examples each.

Appendix B Details on Experimental Setup

B.1 Question Answering

We evaluate each dataset with its standard metric after text normalization: token-level F1 for NarrativeQA and Qasper, and exact match (EM) for DROP, HotpotQA, and MINTEval. For MuSR, we provide all answer options in the input and ask the model to generate one of them, following the same generation format as the other datasets, and compute EM. For MINTEval, we evaluate on the wiki-revision and git-commit. For brevity, we refer to these metrics collectively as accuracy in the paper. We train models for 5 epochs with early stopping. For evaluation, we subsample large test sets (DROP, NarrativeQA, HotpotQA, and MINTEval) to 1.5k due to compute cost.

B.2 Agentic Setup

We report success rate, the fraction of games in which the agent completes the goal within the step limit. For TextWorld, we set the maximum number of steps to 100 and use 1,000 training, 150 validation and 200 test games, generated with non-overlapping random seeds. For BabyAI, we use the official maximum number of steps for each level with 100 instances for each training level (MiniBossLevel) and test levels (PutNextLocal, GoToObjMaze). In the retry experiments (Section 6), the agent is allowed up to 7 attempts per game, with its previous trajectories provided in context. In the demonstration experiments, we run the agent multiple times on each game to build a pool of successful trajectories with varying lengths, and sample five trajectories from this pool as demonstrations. We train the agents using the gold trajectories for 5 epochs with early stopping.

Appendix C Additional Analysis

C.1 Effect of the auxiliary loss weight λ\lambda

Figure 10 shows the success rate of Qwen3.5 on TextWorld Quest as we vary the weight of the auxiliary loss λ\lambda. Adding the auxiliary loss consistently improves over standard SFT (λ=0\lambda=0, 78.5%) for all values of λ\lambda. We use λ=0.25\lambda=0.25, which achieves the best performance, in all experiments unless otherwise specified.

C.2 Agentic Tasks

We examine whether agents can learn from their own failures: when the agent fails to complete a game, it retries the same game up to a maximum number of attempts, with its previous trajectories provided in context. When evaluating over TextWorld, as shown in Figure 10, the auxiliary loss improves the cumulative recovery rate by 19.2% on average. Notably, the standard SFT model tends to converge as the number of attempts increases, whereas the model with the auxiliary loss continues to improve, suggesting that it learns better from past failure trajectories.

C.3 Generalizes to Attention-Based Models

To examine whether our findings generalize to attention-based models, which do not have multiple built-in memory pathways, we provide them with two commonly used forms of memory: textual (Packer et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025) and latent (Mu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024) memory. We conduct the experiment with Qwen3-4B-Instruct model.

C.3.1 Textual & Latent Memory.

For textual memory, we summarize a given document and train the model to generate the answer conditioned on the resulting summary and the question. For latent memory, following prior work (Mu et al., 2024; Ge et al., 2024), we represent each document as a layer-wise KV prefix with KK memory slots. Specifically, we append KK learnable memory tokens to the end of the document and run the resulting sequence through the model. Because these memory tokens follow the document, they can attend to and aggregate information from the preceding tokens. We retain the key-value representations at these KK memory tokens positions from every transformer layer; together, these representations form the latent memory. Training proceeds in two stages: in Stage 1, we train the model to encode document information into these latent memory slots using reasoning supervision. In Stage 2, we provide the latent memory as a prefix cache to the model, which is trained to generate the answer conditioned on the latent memory and the question. The answer-generation loss is backpropagated through the entire computation, including the forward pass used to construct the latent memory.

Textual and Latent Memory Play Complementary Roles.

We compare textual and latent memory under a range of matched memory budgets along two axes: whether the answer appears word-for-word in the context (verbatim vs. non-verbatim) and whether answering requires one or multiple pieces of evidence (single- vs. multi-evidence). See Appendix A for details. As shown in Figure 11, textual memory shows a larger advantage when the required information is directly recoverable (verbatim) or localized in a single piece of evidence (single-evidence), whereas latent memory becomes more competitive when the answer must be inferred (non-verbatim) or requires combining multiple pieces of evidence (multi-evidence). This suggests that textual memory is especially effective when prediction relies on precise information explicitly retained in memory, whereas latent memory is relatively more effective when information must be transformed or aggregated.

C.3.2 Standard SFT Favors Textual Memory over Latent Memory

Naive Hybrid Memory.

For naive hybrid memory, we follow the same Stage 1 as for latent memory, training the model with reasoning supervision to encode document information into the KK latent memory slots. In Stage 2, we provide both the latent memory and textual memory to the model and train it with the same question-answering objective. Thus, both memory representations are jointly available during training, without any additional supervision that explicitly encourages coordination between them.

Analysis.

Figure 8 shows question answering performance with different types of memory, using a textual memory budget of 8k tokens (Wang et al., 2025) and a latent memory budget of 128 slots (Ge et al., 2024). The Oracle, which selects the correct prediction whenever either single-memory model succeeds, measures the complementary information available across the two memories. It outperforms the single-memory models (Text and Latent) by 10.1% on average, indicating that the two memories capture complementary information. However, the model trained with both memories under standard SFT (SFT) remains 7.9% below the Oracle and even falls below the Text (24.1% vs. 25.9%), suggesting that naively combining the two memories does not ensure better coordination or improved performance, and can instead lead them to interfere with each other. These results show that the presence of complementary information across memories does not by itself guarantee effective coordination under joint training.

C.3.3 Adding an Auxiliary Loss to Encourage Latent Memory Use Improves Performance

The previous section shows that naive joint training leads to imbalanced use of the two memory pathways, with the model relying predominantly on textual memory and underutilizing information captured by latent memory. We therefore examine whether an auxiliary objective that explicitly encourages the model to make use of the underutilized latent memory improves memory coordination and overall performance.

Auxiliary Loss for Memory Coordination.

To examine whether encouraging the use of the underutilized latent memory improves memory coordination and, in turn, improves overall performance, we add an auxiliary loss that assigns each memory an explicit role based on its strengths (Appendix C.3.1).

The auxiliary loss encourages the model to use a designated memory pathway by making the other pathway uninformative for the target. For each example ii, the standard hybrid-memory objective is:

ℓ⁡(Ti,Li)=−log⁡pθ​(yi∣qi,Ti,Li),\ell(T_{i},L_{i})=-\log p_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid q_{i},T_{i},L_{i}),

where qiq_{i} and yiy_{i} denote the query and target, and TiT_{i} and LiL_{i} denote the textual and latent memories constructed from the source context of example ii.

We augment the objective with an auxiliary term (ℒiaux\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{aux}}_{i}):

ℒi=ℓ⁡(Ti,Li)+λ​ℒiaux,ℒiaux={ℓ⁡(Ti,sg⁡[Lj]),role⁡(i)=text,ℓ⁡(Tj,Li),role⁡(i)=latent.\mathcal{L}_{i}=\ell(T_{i},L_{i})+\lambda\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{aux}}_{i},\qquad\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{aux}}_{i}=\begin{cases}\ell(T_{i},\operatorname{sg}[L_{j}]),&\mathrm{role}(i)=\mathrm{text},\\ \ell(T_{j},L_{i}),&\mathrm{role}(i)=\mathrm{latent}.\end{cases} (1)

Here, λ\lambda controls the weight of the auxiliary loss, and jj denotes a sampled irrelevant example33 3 To reduce the unrelated factor impact, we sample jj from the same source dataset with a similar document length.. For a text-role example (role⁡(i)=text\mathrm{role}(i)=\mathrm{text}), we keep the correct textual memory TiT_{i} and replace the latent memory with LjL_{j}, so that the model must rely on TiT_{i} to predict yiy_{i}; we stop gradients (sg⁡[⋅]\mathrm{sg}[\cdot]) through LjL_{j} so that this auxiliary term does not update the latent-memory writer. For a latent-role example (role⁡(i)=latent\mathrm{role}(i)=\mathrm{latent}), we instead keep the correct latent memory LiL_{i} and replace the textual memory with TjT_{j}, encouraging the model to preserve and use the target-relevant information through the latent pathway. We use the same λ\lambda to 0.25 for all experiments.

Since the optimal role for each example is not known a priori, we experiment over four criteria for assigning role⁡(i)\mathrm{role}(i). Outcome assigns roles based on which single-memory model answers the example correctly: role⁡(i)=latent\mathrm{role}(i)=\mathrm{latent} if the latent-memory model answers example ii correctly, and role⁡(i)=text\mathrm{role}(i)=\mathrm{text} otherwise. Random assigns each example to the text or latent role uniformly at random. Verbatim follows the distinction identified in Appendix C.3.1, assigning verbatim examples to the text role and non-verbatim examples to the latent role: role⁡(i)=text\mathrm{role}(i)=\mathrm{text} if ii = verbatim else role⁡(i)=latent\mathrm{role}(i)=\mathrm{latent}. Reverse uses the opposite assignment, assigning verbatim examples to the latent role and non-verbatim examples to the text role: role⁡(i)=latent\mathrm{role}(i)=\mathrm{latent} if ii = verbatim else role⁡(i)=text\mathrm{role}(i)=\mathrm{text}.

Results.

We examine whether auxiliary supervision improves coordination between textual and latent memory, and how the criterion used to assign role⁡(i)\mathrm{role}(i) affects this coordination. Table 3 reports accuracy together with the use of each memory (Δ\DeltaLatent and Δ\DeltaText). Standard SFT without auxiliary supervision (Naive) largely ignores latent memory: replacing it with an unrelated one even slightly improves accuracy (Δ\DeltaLatent =−2.4=-2.4).

Role-conditioned supervision. Among the role assignment criteria, Verbatim achieves the best accuracy, improving it from 24.1% to 28.6%, and the largest increase in latent-memory use (−2.4→+4.7-2.4\rightarrow+4.7) while largely preserving textual-memory use (+11.4→+10.4+11.4\rightarrow+10.4). Outcome also improves accuracy (26.1%) but yields a smaller increase in latent-memory use; we hypothesize that per-example correctness is influenced by factors beyond the consistent strengths of each memory, making it a noisier signal for role assignment. Reverse increases latent-memory use only modestly while reducing textual-memory use, and Random does not improve accuracy, showing that the assignment criterion is critical for coordinating the two memories.

Supervision without role assignment. We also apply auxiliary supervision without per-example role assignment: Latent-aux and Text-aux assign all examples to the latent or text role, respectively, and Unrouted applies both auxiliary terms to every example. Latent-aux increases latent-memory use and improves accuracy to 26.1%, but at the cost of textual-memory use, whereas Text-aux mainly increases textual-memory use with little gain in accuracy, and Unrouted improves neither memory use nor accuracy. Together, these results suggest that increasing the use of a single memory can help, but the largest gains come from assigning each example to the memory suited to it, according to the complementary strengths of the two memories.
